To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) the concept of climate as a stationary process is untenable, and that 2) the concept of a climate change as a deviation from a climate state, as commonly understood and defined in the IPCC AR5 WG1 report (see above), is untenable.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of how to define climate and climate change in a way that is consistent with our understanding of the dynamics of the climate system and that is relevant for climate policy.
the definition of climate change in a changing climate, which is the definition of climate in a changing climate.
climate and climate change, and we have defined them in a way that is consistent with the definition of climate and climate variability in the literature.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the definition of climate change as the change in climate over time, as used in the IPCC report, is not only a reasonable definition but also a definition that is in line with the definition of climate as the long term statistics of the weather.
climate change is the change in climate states (averages of macroweather) at time scales longer than the macroweather scale.
climate is a time-averaged state of a system that is in equilibrium with external forcing, and climate change is the change of that time-averaged system.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

we have shown that climate is the average over macroweathers and thus the climate state is defined by the average over macrowaveathers at a scale of 30 years, and that the climate change is the change in climate state at longer time scales.
the climate change is defined as the change in climate state, which is the average of the macroweather over a period, when the macroweater is at its lowest variability.
we have provided a framework to define climate, climate change, and weather in a way that is consistent with the observed variability of the climate system.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the concept of climate is a relative concept, and that the relative reference period is a matter of convention.

climate change should be understood as a change of the climate state, which is the average over a long enough time interval (e.g. 30 years) to capture the variability of the climate at this time scale.
the climate state is a function of the forcing, not just the external forcing but the whole system (including the ocean and land).
